extraction.name: SciQ
extraction.description: A crowdsourced dataset of 13,679 multiple-choice science questions, each with one correct answer and three distractors. Questions were generated from science textbook passages. A smaller direct-answer version provides questions and supporting passages without answer options.
extraction.creator: Johannes Welbl; Nelson F. Liu; Matt Gardner
extraction.citeAs: Johannes Welbl, Nelson F. Liu, and Matt Gardner. Crowdsourcing Multiple Choice Science Questions. arXiv:1707.06209v1 [cs.HC], 19 July 2017.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: A two-stage crowdsourcing process on Amazon Mechanical Turk produced 13,679 questions with a total budget of $10,415. First, workers chose among three filtered science textbook paragraphs, or rejected all three, and wrote a question and correct answer. Selected paragraphs were not reused for further question generation. Second, another worker validated the question-answer pair and supplied three distractors, assisted by six model-generated suggestions. Across the project, 175 workers participated, all required to have Mechanical Turk Master's status. Compensation was $0.30 per HIT for question formulation and $0.20 per HIT for distractor selection.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: A small percentage of supporting passages came from unreleasable texts and were not included in the released direct-answer dataset. Consequently, the direct-answer version is smaller, containing 10,481 training questions, 887 development questions, and 884 test questions. The appendix identifies Barron's New York State Grade 4 Elementary-Level Science Test and Campbell Biology: Concepts & Connections as sources whose documents are not included.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The base corpus consisted of 28 science study textbooks from online learning resources including CK-12, OpenStax, Saylor Foundation, Curriki, and other sources listed in the appendix. These covered biology, chemistry, earth science, and physics, from elementary level to introductory college material. A separate set of 3,705 fourth- and eighth-grade science exam questions was used to train and validate the distractor suggestion model.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The collected questions were randomly shuffled and divided into training, validation, and test sets, with 1,000 questions each in validation and test and the remainder in training. Supporting passages were omitted from the multiple-choice version because the questions were trivial to answer when the original passage was provided. The direct-answer version retained releasable passages and questions but omitted answer options.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A rule-based document filter classified individual sentences and retained paragraphs with a minimum number of accepted sentences. Rules excluded questions and exclamations; sentences without verb phrases; modal or imperative constructions; demonstrative pronouns; non-third-person personal pronouns; pronoun-initial sentences; first names; sentences shorter than 6 or longer than 18 tokens or containing more than two commas; special characters other than punctuation; more than three uppercase-initial tokens; references to graphs, tables, or web links; initial discourse markers; absolute wording; and instructional vocabulary. Workers could reject all three proposed paragraphs if they were irrelevant.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: In the first stage, workers wrote a question answerable from a selected paragraph and supplied its correct answer. Instructions prohibited yes/no and ambiguous questions, required independence from additional context, preferred general principles over highly specific facts, specified question lengths of 6–30 words, and limited answers to three words while preferring shorter answers. In the second stage, another worker judged whether the question could appear in a school science exam and could flag ungrammatical questions, false answers, non-science content, or requirements for highly specific background knowledge. Workers then selected up to two of six model-suggested distractors and wrote at least one themselves, producing three distractors in total. Both tasks provided examples of desirable and undesirable outputs, feedback opportunities, and a contact email.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The second stage validated question-answer pairs and model-generated distractors. Overall, 92.8% of question-answer pairs passed validation. Following an initial pilot, the authors required workers to write at least one distractor themselves because this increased engagement and distractor quality. Model-generated suggestions account for 36.1% of final distractors; acceptance was higher for short answers and almost nonexistent for the few very long answers. A separate qualitative evaluation compared 100 original exam questions with 100 SciQ training questions: evaluators identified the original exam question in 55% of cases, which was not significant at p=0.05 against random guessing.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Two worker stages per question: one worker generated the question and correct answer, and another validated the pair and produced three distractors. The paper does not report repeated independent labels per item.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: A rule-based document filter selected candidate passages. A random-forest distractor ranker implemented in scikit-learn generated the six distractor suggestions shown to workers, using 500 trees and at least four samples per leaf. Its features included GloVe embeddings, grammatical and lexical consistency measures, WordNet relationships, and knowledge-base connections derived from OpenIE triples extracted from Simple Wikipedia.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The corpus targets school science and introductory college science rather than a broad general domain. The direct-answer release excludes passages from unreleasable sources and is therefore smaller than the multiple-choice release. The authors report that some irrelevant paragraphs remained after filtering. Automatically suggested distractors were not reliable enough for use without human filtering: they could have incorrect semantic types, mismatched specificity, or unrelated or ungrammatical multiword expressions.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing of science question-answering and reading-comprehension systems. In the multiple-choice setting, systems select the correct answer and must obtain their own background information. In the direct-answer setting, systems predict the answer span from a supplied passage and question. SciQ is intended for research on neural models in medium-sized data settings and as additional training data for answering real science exams; adding it improved evaluated models' performance on fourth- and eighth-grade exam questions.
